summary: This standards-track RFC specifies version 3 of the RPCSEC_GSS Remote Procedure Call security protocol. It supports multi-principal authentication, security label assertions, structured privilege assertions and channel bindings. It updates RFC 5403.

plainLanguage.summary: RPCSEC_GSS is the security layer of the Remote Procedure Call protocol, which is how a program on one machine calls a program on another. Version 3 lets the client say more about itself to the server: that a user and a machine are both involved, what security level the calling process runs at, and what special permission it wants. The server checks those claims and decides what to allow.

questions: how does multi-principal authentication work in rpc
what is the rpcsec_gss child handle
subtitle: Lets an RPC client tell the server more about who is calling and what they are allowed.

tldr.problem: RPCSEC_GSS version 2 lets a client prove who it is, but it gives the client no way to say anything more. A server that wants to know both which user is calling and which machine is acting for that user, or that the calling process runs at a particular security level, or that it holds a special application privilege, has no way to learn any of that.
tldr.mechanism: Version 3 adds a create procedure. The client asks the server for a child context handle and attaches one or more assertions to it: a second security context for the user, a security label, a structured privilege, or a channel binding. The server checks them and returns the child handle with the accepted assertions enumerated.
tldr.outcome: The server can make authorization decisions that depend on the identity of the user, the trust of the client host, the security level of the calling process, or an application-defined privilege. The document also replaces the old channel-binding operation and adds a new reply verifier that closes a man-in-the-middle gap.

today: RFC 7861 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2016. It updates RFC 5403, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or further updates it. The file system protocol that uses it is RFC 7862.

sections.title: What RPCSEC_GSSv3 Adds
sections.content:
RPCSEC_GSS version 3 is the same as RPCSEC_GSS version 2 except that several assertions of authority have been added: security labels for Full Mode security type enforcement and other labelled security models; application-specific structured privileges, which let an RPC application client pass structured information to the corresponding application code in a server so that the privilege and the conditions in which it may be exercised are controlled; multi-principal authentication of the client host and the user to the server, done by binding two RPCSEC_GSS handles; and simplified channel binding.

Assertions of labels and privileges are evaluated by the server, which may then map the asserted values to other values according to server-side policy. An option for enumerating the server-supported Label Format Specifiers is provided as well.

There is no RPCSEC_GSS_CREATE payload that is REQUIRED to implement: RPCSEC_GSSv3 implementations are feature driven. Besides the create operation and payloads for the features they want, every implementation MUST implement the new version number, the new reply verifier and the new auth_stat values. An implementation that targets a given feature MUST also implement the list operation, and the create operation replies for unsupported features in a defined way: a label assertion that is not supported gives the new RPCSEC_GSS_LABEL_PROBLEM status, a structured privilege assertion that is not supported gives RPCSEC_GSS_UNKNOWN_MESSAGE, and for multi-principal authentication and channel bindings the target simply leaves the corresponding field out of the reply.
sections.plainLanguage: RPCSEC_GSS is the security layer of the Remote Procedure Call protocol, which is how a program on one machine calls a program on another. Version 3 lets the client say more about itself to the server: that a user and a machine are both involved, what security level the calling process runs at, and what special permission it wants. The server checks those claims and decides what to allow.

sections.title: Parent and Child Handles
sections.content:
RPCSEC_GSSv3 is very similar to version 2, and the whole protocol is not restated; only the differences are shown. The new support for assertions and channel bindings is implemented through a different mechanism: a client uses an existing RPCSEC_GSSv3 context handle, established in the usual manner, to protect the exchange. That handle is called the parent handle. The server issues a child RPCSEC_GSSv3 handle in the RPCSEC_GSS_CREATE response, and the child handle uses the underlying GSS-API security context of the parent handle in all subsequent exchanges. A child handle MUST NOT be used as the parent handle in an RPCSEC_GSS_CREATE control message.

All the functionality of version 2 is supported, with one exception: the RPCSEC_GSS_BIND_CHANNEL operation is not supported on version 3 handles, because version 3 provides a channel-binding assertion instead. If a server receives a BIND_CHANNEL operation on a version 3 handle, it MUST reply with MSG_ACCEPTED and an accept_stat of PROC_UNAVAIL.

Version negotiation is done with the rgc_version field. An initiator that supports version 3 issues an RPCSEC_GSS request with that field set to RPCSEC_GSS_VERS_3, and a target that does not recognise it returns an RPC error. The initiator MUST NOT use a handle returned by version 3 of a target with version 1 or version 2 of the same target, and MUST NOT use a handle returned by version 1 or version 2 with version 3 of the same target.
sections.plainLanguage: The client keeps the security context it already has, and the server hands back a second, narrower handle that carries the extra claims. Everything the client says afterwards is protected with the original context, but the claims travel with the new handle, so the server can tell which claims belong to which call.

sections.title: The New Reply Verifier
sections.content:
A new reply verifier is needed because a child and a parent handle share the same GSS context, and so could have the same RPCSEC_GSS sequence numbers. The reply verifier of earlier versions computes a Message Integrity Code on just the sequence number, which provides opportunities for man-in-the-middle attacks.

Version 3 addresses this by computing the verifier with exactly the same input as the request verifier, except that the mtype is changed from CALL to REPLY. The new reply verifier computes a MIC over the RPC reply header: the transaction identifier, the message type set to REPLY, the RPC version, the program number, the version number, the procedure number and the credential, which is what binds the RPCSEC_GSS handle.
sections.plainLanguage: Because two handles share one underlying security context, the old way of protecting a reply, which covered only the sequence number, could be replayed or swapped. The new way protects the whole reply header, including the handle that identifies which security context the reply belongs to.

sections.title: Multi-Principal Authentication
sections.content:
A client MAY assert a multi-principal authentication of the RPC client host principal and a user principal. The feature is needed when an RPC client host wants to use authority assertions that the server may only grant if a user and a client host are authenticated together. A server may refuse to grant requested authority to a user acting alone, for example through an unprivileged user-space program, or to an RPC client host acting alone, but may grant it to a client host acting on behalf of a user if the server identifies the user and trusts the client host. It is assumed that an unprivileged user-space program would not have access to the client host credentials needed to establish a GSS-API security context authenticating the client host, so such a program could not create a message that successfully binds a host and a user context.

In addition to the parent handle, the call data has a second handle, the inner handle, referenced through the rgmp_handle field. The parent handle must correspond to a GSS-API security context that authenticates the client host, and the inner handle must correspond to one that authenticates the user; the reverse MUST NOT be used. The child handle returned by a successful multi-principal assertion binds the inner handle to the parent handle, and servers MUST treat it as authenticating the principal that the inner context authenticated, which may be mapped to a server-side notion of user.

Multi-principal binding is done by including an assertion of type rgss3_gss_mp_auth in the create call data, with the inner handle in the rgmp_handle field and a MIC of the RPC header up to and including the credential in the rgmp_rpcheader_mic field. The create procedure with a multi-principal payload MUST use the rpc_gss_svc_privacy service, so that an attacker cannot intercept the procedure, reassign the parent context handle and steal the user's identity.

The target verifies the assertion by first confirming that the parent context used is a client host context, then verifying the MIC with the security context associated with the inner handle. On success the reply carries the inner handle and a MIC over the RPC reply header. On failure the field is left out and a MSG_DENIED reply is formulated as usual: a missing context for the parent handle gives the existing RPCSEC_GSS_CREDPROBLEM, while a missing context for the inner handle or a MIC that does not verify gives the new RPCSEC_GSS_INNER_CREDPROBLEM.
sections.plainLanguage: The claim is that a person and a machine are both involved: the machine is trusted, and the person is who they say they are. The client proves the machine first, then proves the person with a second security context, and sends a checksum over both. The server checks both, and the whole exchange is encrypted so that nobody can swap the machine's identity in between.

sections.title: Channel Binding
sections.content:
Version 3 does channel binding differently from version 2. It reuses existing, established context handles rather than providing a separate RPC security flavour for establishing them, and the channel-bindings data is not hashed, because there is now general agreement that it is the secure channel's responsibility to produce channel-bindings data of manageable size.

The client prefixes the channel-bindings data octet string with the channel type, then calls GSS_GetMIC to get a MIC of the resulting octet string using the parent handle's GSS-API security context, and places the MIC in the rca_chan_bind_mic field of the create arguments. If that field is set, the server MUST verify the client's channel-binding MIC if it supports the feature. If verification succeeds, the server MUST generate a new MIC over the same channel bindings and place it in the reply; if verification fails or the server does not support channel binding, it says so by leaving the field out. The client MUST verify the returned MIC by calling GSS_VerifyMIC with the MIC and the channel-bindings data, including the channel-type prefix. If that verification fails the client MUST call RPCSEC_GSS_DESTROY. If the client asked for channel binding and the server did not include a MIC, the client MAY continue to use the handle as though channel binding had never been requested, unless it considers channel binding critical, in which case it MUST call RPCSEC_GSS_DESTROY.
sections.plainLanguage: Channel binding ties the security context to the connection underneath it, so that a stolen request cannot be replayed on a different connection. The client takes a value that identifies the connection, signs it with the security context, and sends it with the request. The server checks it and signs the same value back, and the client checks that too.

sections.title: Labels and Structured Privileges
sections.content:
A label assertion carries a subject label in a given Label Format Specifier. The client discovers which formats the server supports through the RPCSEC_GSS_LIST control message. The LFS is an identifier used to establish the syntactic format of the security label and the semantic meaning of its components, and the Policy Identifier is an optional part of an LFS that lets clients and the server identify specific security policies. The label encoding mirrors the NFSv4.2 sec_label attribute, and Full Mode MAC is enabled when a version 3 process subject label assertion is combined with a file object label provided by that attribute.

If a label itself needs privacy protection, the client MUST use the rpc_gss_svc_privacy service for the create request. The label assertion payload is the set of subject labels asserted by the calling NFS client process, and the resulting child context is used for NFS requests asserting those labels. Servers that support labelling in the requested format MAY map the requested subject label to a different one as a result of server-side policy. The labels accepted by the target must be enumerated in the reply. Servers that do not support labelling, or do not support the requested format, reject the assertion with an auth_stat of RPCSEC_GSS_LABEL_PROBLEM.

A structured privilege is a capability defined by a specific RPC application. The application may define a private data structure that clients and servers implementing it understand, and the client asserts the privilege by including an assertion of type rgss3_privs in the create call data. The privilege is identified by a description string, and the private data travels as opaque data in the rp_privilege field, so that the RPCSEC_GSS layer does not need to know the details of the structure. The encoding, the server verification and any server policies for structured privileges are described by the RPC application definition. A successful assertion must be enumerated in the reply. An assertion the server does not recognise is rejected with an auth_stat of RPCSEC_GSS_UNKNOWN_MESSAGE, and a request containing unsupported assertions is rejected with RPCSEC_GSS_PRIVILEGE_PROBLEM. A server MUST NOT reject a request containing supported privilege assertions even if some of those assertions are rejected for local policy reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of extra claim can be attached to the handle. A security label says what level the calling process runs at, in a format the server and client have agreed on. A structured privilege is something only the application understands, such as permission to copy a file from one server to another, and it travels as a name plus a blob of data that the RPC layer passes along without interpreting.

sections.title: Deployment Recommendation
sections.content:
RPCSEC_GSSv3 is a superset of version 2, which is in turn a superset of version 1, so it can be used in all situations where version 2 is used, or where version 1 is used and channel-bindings functionality is not needed. It should be used when the new functionality is needed.

The version 3 control messages resemble the version 1 and 2 DESTROY control message in that the sequence number in the request must be valid and the header checksum in the verifier must be valid. As in the earlier versions, control messages may contain call data following the verifier in the body of the NULLPROC procedure, so they look a lot like an RPCSEC_GSS data message with the header procedure set to NULLPROC. The client MUST use either the integrity or the privacy service to protect the CREATE or LIST control message, and MUST NOT use the none service.
sections.plainLanguage: Version 3 keeps everything version 2 could do, except the old channel-binding operation, which it replaces. A site can run version 3 everywhere that version 2 ran, and fall back to version 2 only where the older clients are.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The whole document deals with security issues. RPCSEC_GSSv3 allows clients to assert data that is relevant to the server's authorization decisions, and those assertions must be evaluated by the server in the context of whether the client and the user are authenticated, whether multi-principal authentication was used, whether the client is trusted, what ranges of assertions are allowed for the client and the user separately or together, and any relevant server-side policy. The security semantics of the assertions are specific to the application protocol.

RPCSEC_GSSv3 is not a complete solution for labelling: it conveys the labels of actors but not the labels of objects, so an RPC application protocol may have to be extended to carry object label information.

There may be interactions with the NFSv4 callback security scheme and with the NFSv4.1 GSS SSV mechanism. The NFSv4 callback scheme requires the server to initiate GSS-API security contexts, which does not work well in practice, and in the case of client-side processes running as the same user but with different privileges and security labels it seems particularly unlikely to work well. The NFSv4.1 scheme lacks those problems, but it is important that the server pick an appropriate context handle for callbacks, and in particular that it use handles that authenticate the client to protect callbacks related to server state initiated by calls protected by version 3 contexts.
sections.plainLanguage: The server has to judge each claim on its own terms: who is authenticated, whether the client host is trusted, and what the local policy allows. The RFC is also clear about the limit of the scheme. It carries the security level of the people making the call, but not the security level of the files they are trying to reach, so the file system protocol has to supply that part.

viz.caption: THE FOUR CLAIMS A CLIENT CAN NOW ATTACH

columns: What it lets the server do

cells: A second security context for the user, alongside the parent context for the client host
Grant authority only when a host and a user are both authenticated
A subject label in a format the server supports
Apply a multi-level security policy to the request
A named privilege with application-defined data
Authorize the operation, subject to the application's own policy
A MIC over the transport channel's binding data
Confirm the call arrived over the same channel the client used
